prompt: The node being splayed has no grandparent — its parent is the root. Which case applies?
options: Zig — a single rotation around the parent
Zig-Zig — rotate around the grandparent first, then the parent
Zig-Zag — rotate around the parent first, then the grandparent
None — splaying stops when the grandparent is missing
explanation: Zig is the single-rotation case that applies exactly when no grandparent exists. It occurs at most once per splay, as the final step that lifts the node into the root position.

prompt: Node w and its parent p are both left children of their respective parents. Which case applies, and in what order are the rotations performed?
options: Zig-Zig: rotate around the grandparent g first, then around p
Zig-Zig: rotate around p first, then around g
Zig-Zag: rotate around p first, then around g
Zig: a single rotation around p
explanation: Same side (both left or both right) = Zig-Zig. The *farther* node — the grandparent — is rotated first, then the parent. That order is exactly what distinguishes Zig-Zig from two independent Zig steps, which would leave a different, less balanced tree.

prompt: Node w is a left child of p, and p is a right child of g. Which case applies, and in what order are the rotations performed?
options: Zig-Zag: rotate around p first, then around g
Zig-Zig: rotate around g first, then around p
Zig-Zag: rotate around g first, then around p
Zig: a single rotation around g
explanation: Opposite sides = Zig-Zag, and here the *nearer* node (the parent p) is rotated first, then the grandparent g. Note the rotation order is the mirror image of Zig-Zig's — that contrast is the most frequently examined detail of splaying.

prompt: The three splay cases — which two statements are correct?
options: Zig occurs at most once per splay, namely as the final step.
Zig-Zig rotates the farther node (g) first, Zig-Zag the nearer node (p) first.
Zig-Zig and Zig-Zag use the same rotation order; only the sides differ.
Which case applies is determined by the key being searched for, not by the node's position.
explanation: Zig can only fire when the parent is already the root, hence at most once and last ✓, and the differing rotation order is the defining contrast ✓✗. The case is chosen purely from the geometric relation of node, parent and grandparent ✗.

prompt: A splay-tree search does not find the key. Which statement is correct?
options: The last node visited before falling out of the tree is splayed to the root anyway.
Nothing happens — only successful searches trigger a splay.
The tree is rebuilt from scratch.
An error is raised and the tree is left in an inconsistent state.
explanation: Splaying happens on *every* access, successful or not — the last real node examined becomes the new root. This is exactly what makes the tree self-adjusting, and it is also why splay-tree delete begins with a find that has already moved the relevant node to the root.

prompt: Complexity of splay trees — which two statements are correct?
options: Insert, search and delete are O(log n) amortized.
A single operation can still cost O(n) in the worst case.
Every single operation is O(log n), worst case included.
Repeated access to the same key costs Θ(log n) each time.
explanation: The potential-function argument gives O(log n) amortized ✓, while one splay can traverse an entire n-node path ⟹ O(n) for a single operation ✓✗. Repeated access to the same key is O(1) amortized, since the key is already at the root ✗.

prompt: Splay trees compared with AVL and Red-Black trees — which two statements are correct?
options: Splay trees store no balance metadata at all — no heights, no colours, no balance factors.
Splay trees restructure the tree even on a pure lookup, which AVL and RB trees do not.
Splay trees maintain a balance factor per node, just like AVL trees.
Splay trees guarantee a height of at most 2·log(n+1).
explanation: The absence of stored metadata ✓ and restructuring on read ✓ are the two defining differences. Options 3 and 4 both describe guarantees splay trees deliberately give up ✗✗ — there is no worst-case height bound, only an amortized one.

prompt: Splay-tree delete of a key that is present — which two statements are correct?
options: The initial find splays the node to the root, so the node to be deleted is the root when it is removed.
After removing the root, the maximum of the left subtree L is splayed to L's root; since it has no right child, R can be attached there directly.
After removing the root, the minimum of the left subtree L is splayed up and R attached as its left child.
If L is empty the delete fails and the tree must be rebuilt.
explanation: find always splays, so deletion always happens at the root ✓, and the *maximum* of L provably has no right child, which is exactly the free slot R needs ✓. The minimum would have no *left* child, which is the wrong side ✗, and an empty L is trivial — R simply becomes the new tree ✗.
